blocks.cap: Each small square is one hundredth of the grid, and \(37\) of them are shaded, so the shaded count and the percent are the same number. The same amount is \(\frac{37}{100}\) as a fraction and \(0.37\) as a decimal. The \(100\) squares are what the \(37\) is counted against, and renaming the shaded part does not change how much is shaded.

blocks.x: A percent question names three numbers, an amount, a percent, and the whole the percent is taken of. The sentence \(a\) is \(p\%\) of \(b\) says \(a\) equals \(\frac{p}{100}\) of \(b\), and of means multiply, so the sentence is \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\). Two of the three are given and one is the letter. The next two problems leave out a different one.

A vineyard has 875 vines and \(24\%\) of them are a new cultivar. Here \(p=24\) and \(b=875\), and the amount \(a\) is missing. Substitute into \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\) and enter the number of new-cultivar vines.
hints: \(24\%\) is the number \(\frac{24}{100}\), and of means multiply, so the count is \(\frac{24}{100}\) times \(875\).
\(\frac{24}{100}\) reduces to \(\frac{6}{25}\), and \(875\div 25=35\), so divide before multiplying.
blocks.sol: \(a=\frac{24}{100}(875)=\frac{6}{25}(875)=6(35)=\boxed{210}\). Reducing \(\frac{24}{100}\) first turns the work into \(875\div 25\) and \(6\times 35\), shorter than multiplying \(875\) by \(24\) and then dividing by \(100\).

blocks.x: A hall has 650 seats and 273 of them are booked. This time \(a=273\) and \(b=650\) are known and \(p\) is missing. Solve \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\) for \(p\) and enter the percent of the seats booked, just the number.
hints: Substituting gives \(273=\frac{p}{100}(650)\), and multiplying both sides by \(100\) clears the fraction.
That leaves \(650p=27300\), a one-letter equation of the kind 4.2 solves in one division.
blocks.sol: From \(273=\frac{p}{100}(650)\), multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(650p=27300\), so \(p=\boxed{42}\). Dividing part by whole gives the same number, since \(\frac{273}{650}=0.42\) and \(0.42\times 100=42\).

blocks.x: The percent equation, \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\). The sentence \(a\) is \(p\%\) of \(b\) is that equation, with \(b\) the base, \(a\) the amount compared against it, and \(p\) the percent. Any two of the three are enough to find the third. With \(p\) and \(b\) given, multiply. With \(a\) and \(b\) given, \(p=\frac{100a}{b}\). With \(a\) and \(p\) given, \(b=\frac{100a}{p}\). Each rearrangement is chapter 4 work on a one-letter linear equation, so there is one equation here and not three separate rules.

The third case goes wrong most often. In \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\) the base is the quantity being multiplied, so when the base is what is missing the equation has to be undone rather than run forward. The next two problems are both of that kind, and each one names the number the wrong route produces.

At a theatre, 350 seats are sold, and that is \(28\%\) of the seats in the house. A student computes \(28\%\) of \(350\) and reports a house of \(98\) seats. Enter the correct number of seats in the house.
accept: one thousand two hundred and fifty
hints: The \(28\%\) is taken of the whole house, so the house is the whole \(b\) and the \(350\) is the amount \(a\).
\(350=\frac{28}{100}b\), and multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(35000=28b\).
blocks.sol: From \(350=\frac{28}{100}b\), multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(28b=35000\), so \(b=\boxed{1250}\). Since \(350\) is the part rather than the whole, the correct move is to divide by \(\frac{28}{100}\) instead of multiplying, and \(98\) is smaller than the \(350\) seats already sold.

blocks.x: Augustus levied the centesima rerum venalium, a hundredth on the price of goods sold at auction, to fund army pensions. Roman clerks were computing in hundredths for centuries before there was a percent sign.

An inspector passes \(62\%\) of a shipment and sets the other 209 items aside. The 209 is not the \(62\%\) part, so work out what percent of the shipment it is before writing the equation. Enter the number of items in the shipment.
hints: The whole shipment is \(100\%\) of itself, and the set-aside items are what is left once the passing \(62\%\) is taken out.
The set-aside items are \(38\%\), so the equation is \(209=\frac{38}{100}b\).
blocks.sol: The set-aside items are \(100-62=38\) percent of the shipment, so \(209=\frac{38}{100}b\) gives \(38b=20900\) and \(b=\boxed{550}\). Dividing \(209\) by \(0.62\) instead pairs the count with the wrong percent and gives about \(337\). The check is \(\frac{62}{100}(550)=341\), the number that passed, and \(341+209=550\).

blocks.x: Finding the base is a division. In \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\) the base is multiplied by \(\frac{p}{100}\), so multiplying both sides by \(\frac{100}{p}\) leaves \(b=\frac{100a}{p}\). Multiplying the part by the percent instead computes \(\frac{p}{100}a\), the answer to a different question, what \(p\%\) of the part is. For \(p\) below \(100\) that product is smaller than \(a\), and a base is never smaller than a part of itself, so the size alone is enough to reject it. The check is one multiplication, since \(\frac{p}{100}\) of the answer has to come to \(a\).

The same amount is a different percent of different bases, and one percent taken against different bases gives different amounts. Fifteen percent of \(200\) is \(30\), and fifteen percent of \(800\) is \(120\). When a story states two totals, each percent belongs to the total its own sentence names, and adding the two gives a percent of neither.

A cannery runs two filling lines. The morning line fills 720 tins and \(45\%\) of them hold soup. The afternoon line fills 450 tins and \(16\%\) of them hold soup. Each percent is taken of its own line's run. Enter the total number of tins of soup.
hints: The \(45\%\) is taken of the morning run only and the \(16\%\) of the afternoon run only, so the two bases are different and the counts have to be worked out separately.
The morning count is \(\frac{45}{100}(720)\), and the afternoon count is the same form with \(16\) as the percent and \(450\) as the base.
blocks.sol: The morning count is \(\frac{45}{100}(720)=324\) and the afternoon count is \(\frac{16}{100}(450)=72\), so the total is \(324+72=\boxed{396}\). Adding the percents and taking \(61\%\) of all \(1170\) tins gives \(713.7\), which is wrong because neither percent was measured against \(1170\).

blocks.x: A car park holds only vans and cars, 96 vans and 384 cars. Enter the percent of all the vehicles in the car park that are vans, just the number.
hints: The comparison is against every vehicle in the car park, and that total is not printed in the problem.
The whole is \(96+384=480\), so the equation is \(96=\frac{p}{100}(480)\).
blocks.sol: The car park holds \(96+384=480\) vehicles, so \(96=\frac{p}{100}(480)\) gives \(480p=9600\) and \(p=\boxed{20}\). Taking \(384\) as the whole instead gives \(25\), which is 6.1's part-to-part comparison rather than a share of every vehicle.

blocks.x: The base is what follows the word of. In \(a\) is \(p\%\) of \(b\), the quantity named after of is \(b\), and \(b\) is the quantity \(\frac{p}{100}\) is multiplied by. Swapping the two changes the answer, since \(\frac{100a}{b}\) and \(\frac{100b}{a}\) are equal only when \(a=b\). When a story gives two parts and no total, the base for a share of the whole is their sum and not the other part. When it gives two totals, each percent has its own base, so one percent of the combined total is a different quantity from either.

The equation \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\) holds for any \(p\), not only for \(p\) between \(1\) and \(100\). With \(p\) above \(100\), \(\frac{p}{100}\) is greater than \(1\), so the amount comes out larger than the base. With \(p\) below \(1\), \(\frac{p}{100}\) is smaller than \(\frac{1}{100}\), so the base is more than a hundred times the amount.
Depot A holds 2380 tonnes of grain, which is \(175\%\) of what Depot B holds. Here \(\frac{175}{100}\) is greater than \(1\). Enter the number of tonnes Depot B holds.
accept: one thousand three hundred and sixty
hints: The 2380 tonnes is compared against what Depot B holds, so Depot B is the base. Call that base \(b\).
blocks.sol: Depot B is the base, so \(2380=\frac{175}{100}b=\frac{7}{4}b\). Multiplying both sides by \(4\) gives \(7b=9520\), so \(b=\boxed{1360}\). With a percent above \(100\) the amount is larger than the base, so any answer above 2380 would be wrong.

blocks.x: A quarry's tailings are \(0.15\%\) recoverable metal by mass, and that metal weighs 42 tonnes. Of those same tailings, 5040 tonnes have already been shipped to a second site. Enter what percent of the total tailings mass has been shipped, just the number.
hints: \(0.15\%\) is \(\frac{0.15}{100}\), which is \(0.0015\), and the metal is that fraction of all the tailings, so the tailings mass is a missing base.
Multiplying \(42=\frac{0.15}{100}b\) by \(100\) gives \(0.15b=4200\), so \(b\) comes out by dividing by \(0.15\). With \(b\) known, solve \(5040=\frac{p}{100}b\) for \(p\).
blocks.sol: From \(42=\frac{0.15}{100}b\), multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(0.15b=4200\), so \(b=28000\) tonnes, and then \(5040=\frac{p}{100}(28000)\) gives \(28000p=504000\) and \(p=\boxed{18}\). Since the percent is below \(1\), the base is more than a hundred times the amount, which is why 42 tonnes of metal comes from 28000 tonnes of tailings.

blocks.x: Every question here was \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\) with a different one of the three letters unknown, and the work each time was deciding which number is the base. Lesson 6.4, Percent Problems, keeps that equation and takes up the case where a quantity rises or falls by a percent, and the base there is what the quantity was before the change.

review.x: Write \(85\%\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Percent means per hundred, so \(85\%\) is \(\frac{85}{100}\) before any reducing.
Any number ending in \(0\) or \(5\) is divisible by \(5\), and both \(85\) and \(100\) end that way.
review.sol: Dividing numerator and denominator of \(\frac{85}{100}\) by \(5\) gives \(\boxed{\frac{17}{20}}\). Since \(17\) is prime and \(20\) is not a multiple of \(17\), no further reducing is possible.

review.x: Write \(9\%\) as a decimal.
hints: The percent sign means per hundred, so \(9\%=\frac{9}{100}\). The decimal you want is the value of \(9\div 100\).
\(9\) divided by \(100\) is less than \(1\), so the answer starts with a zero in front of the decimal point. Multiply your answer by \(100\) as a check and \(9\) should come back.
review.sol: \(9\%\) is \(\frac{9}{100}\), so move the decimal point in \(9.0\) two places left to divide by \(100\), which gives \(9\%=\boxed{0.09}\). One place left would give \(0.9\), and that is \(90\%\).

review.x: A pressure gauge reads \(0.58\) of full scale. Enter that reading as a percent, just the number.
hints: Percent means per hundred, so the question is how many hundredths the reading is worth.
To turn a decimal into a percent, multiply by \(100\), which moves the decimal point two places to the right.
review.sol: Multiplying by \(100\) gives \(0.58\times 100=\boxed{58}\). Two decimal places means hundredths, so \(0.58=\frac{58}{100}\), which is \(58\) per hundred.

review.x: A crate is \(\frac{13}{25}\) full. Rewrite that ratio with \(100\) below the bar and enter the percent, just the number.
hints: Multiplying both parts of a ratio by the same number leaves it unchanged, and \(25\) has to reach \(100\).
The factor is \(4\), so multiply \(13\) by \(4\) as well.
review.sol: Multiplying both parts by \(4\) gives \(\frac{13}{25}=\frac{52}{100}\), so the percent is \(\boxed{52}\).

review.x: A battery loses \(2.4\%\) of its charge overnight. Write \(2.4\%\) as a decimal.
hints: A percent is a count per hundred whether or not the number is whole, so \(2.4\%\) means \(\frac{2.4}{100}\).
Dividing by \(100\) slides the decimal point two places to the left. Since \(2.4\) has only one digit left of the point, you write a placeholder zero in the empty place.
review.sol: Dividing by \(100\) slides the decimal point two places to the left, so \(2.4\%=\frac{2.4}{100}=\boxed{0.024}\). One hop left of \(2.4\) gives \(0.24\), and \(0.24\) is \(24\%\), so the second hop is the one that matters.

review.x: A service fee is \(7.5\%\) of an order. Write \(7.5\%\) as a fraction in lowest terms, in the form \(a/b\).
hints: A percent is a count out of \(100\), so start from \(\frac{7.5}{100}\) and clear the decimal by multiplying top and bottom by \(10\).
That gives \(\frac{75}{1000}\), and \(75\) and \(1000\) share a factor of \(25\).
review.sol: Multiplying top and bottom of \(\frac{7.5}{100}\) by \(10\) gives \(\frac{75}{1000}\), and dividing both by \(25\) gives \(\boxed{\frac{3}{40}}\). Multiplying top and bottom by the same number never changes the value, so \(\frac{7.5}{100}\) and \(\frac{3}{40}\) are the same number.

review.x: A kiln fires \(\frac{4}{9}\) of a load at a time. Since \(9\) does not divide \(100\), that share is not a whole number of percent. Enter it as an exact percent, written as a single fraction in lowest terms rather than a mixed number or a rounded decimal.
hints: A percent is a count of hundredths, so the share as a percent is the number \(p\) for which \(\frac{p}{100}=\frac{4}{9}\).
That \(p\) is \(\frac{4}{9}\times 100\). Multiplying by \(100\) multiplies the numerator by \(100\) and leaves the denominator at \(9\), so check whether the fraction that results reduces.
review.sol: A percent is a count of hundredths, so the number of percent is \(\frac{4}{9}\times 100=\boxed{\frac{400}{9}}\). The numerator \(400\) and the denominator \(9\) have no common factor other than \(1\), so that is lowest terms, and the decimal form \(44.444\ldots\) does not terminate, which makes \(44.4\%\) a rounding and not the exact share.

review.x: A depot stores 840 tyres and \(65\%\) of them are winter tyres. Enter the number of winter tyres.
hints: The \(65\%\) is taken of all \(840\) tyres, so \(840\) is the base and the count is the missing \(a\).

review.x: A tank holds 1600 litres of brine, and \(3.5\%\) of it is salt. Enter the number of litres of salt.
hints: A percent that is not a whole number still goes over \(100\), so \(3.5\%\) is \(\frac{3.5}{100}\).
\(\frac{3.5}{100}=0.035\), and the base is the full \(1600\) litres.

review.x: A polling office mails out 700 survey forms, and 189 of them come back. Enter what percent of the forms came back, just the number.
hints: Percent means per hundred, so the answer is the numerator \(p\) that makes \(\frac{p}{100}\) equal to the fraction of forms that came back. The base is all \(700\) forms sent, not the \(189\) returned.
Dividing both sides of \(189=\frac{p}{100}(700)\) by \(700\) leaves \(\frac{p}{100}=\frac{189}{700}\), so cancel a factor of \(7\) from \(\frac{189}{700}\) to put \(100\) below the bar.
review.sol: Let \(p\) be the percent, so \(189=\frac{p}{100}(700)\). Multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(700p=18900\), so \(p=\boxed{27}\). Checking, \(\frac{27}{100}\) of \(700\) is \(27\times 7=189\).

review.x: A shelf holds 640 books, 80 of them reference books. Enter what percent of the books on the shelf are reference books, just the number.
hints: The reference books are compared against every book on the shelf, so \(640\) is the base.
\(\frac{80}{640}=\frac{1}{8}\), and \(\frac{1}{8}\) of \(100\) is not a whole number.
review.sol: From \(80=\frac{p}{100}(640)\), multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(640p=8000\), so \(p=\boxed{12.5}\). A percent need not be a whole number.

review.x: A deposit of 144 dollars is \(32\%\) of a fee. Enter the fee in dollars.
hints: The fee is the unknown here, so call it \(b\). The \(32\%\) is a percent of the fee and not of \(144\), so \(b\) is the base and \(144\) is the part.
\(144=\frac{32}{100}b\) becomes \(32b=14400\) once both sides are multiplied by \(100\).
review.sol: From \(144=\frac{32}{100}b\), multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(32b=14400\), so \(b=\boxed{450}\). Checking, \(\frac{32}{100}(450)=144\).

review.x: A club has 78 members who have paid their dues, and that is \(26\%\) of the membership. Multiplying \(78\) by \(26\%\) gives \(20.28\), fewer people than have already paid. Enter the number of members in the club.
hints: The \(26\%\) is taken of the whole membership, so the membership is the base and the \(78\) is the part. Finding a base from a part is a division, not a multiplication.
Call the membership \(b\). Then \(78=\frac{26}{100}b\), and multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(26b=7800\).
review.sol: With \(b\) the number of members, \(78=\frac{26}{100}b\), and multiplying both sides by \(100\) gives \(26b=7800\), so \(b=\boxed{300}\). The \(20.28\) is \(26\%\) of the part, and a club is never smaller than the number of members who have paid.

review.x: Depot X ships 250 crates and \(24\%\) of them are fragile. Depot Y ships 380 crates and \(15\%\) of them are fragile. Enter the number of fragile crates the two depots ship together.
hints: Each percent is taken of its own depot's crates, so the two bases are different and the counts have to be worked out separately.
\(\frac{24}{100}(250)=60\), and the second count is the same equation with \(380\) as the base.
review.sol: The counts are \(\frac{24}{100}(250)=60\) and \(\frac{15}{100}(380)=57\), so the total is \(60+57=\boxed{117}\). The two percents cannot be added, because \(24\%\) is taken of \(250\) crates and \(15\%\) of \(380\) crates, and \(39\%\) of all \(630\) crates would be \(245.7\).

review.x: A tank has a capacity of 3060 litres, which is \(120\%\) of a second tank's capacity. Enter the capacity of the second tank in litres.
accept: two thousand five hundred and fifty
hints: The \(120\%\) is taken of the second tank, so the second tank is the base \(b\) and \(3060\) is the amount.
review.sol: From \(3060=\frac{120}{100}b=\frac{6}{5}b\), multiplying both sides by \(5\) gives \(6b=15300\), so \(b=\boxed{2550}\). A percent above \(100\) means the first tank is the larger of the two, so the answer had to be less than \(3060\), and \(1.2(2550)=3060\) checks.

review.x: In a batch of 45000 screws, \(0.24\%\) are out of tolerance. Enter the number of screws out of tolerance.
hints: A percent is divided by \(100\) whether or not it is below \(1\), so \(0.24\%\) is \(\frac{0.24}{100}\).
\(\frac{0.24}{100}=0.0024\), not \(0.24\), and the count is that decimal times \(45000\).
review.sol: \(0.24\%=\frac{0.24}{100}=0.0024\), so the count is \(0.0024(45000)=\boxed{108}\). Using \(0.24\) instead gives \(10800\), which is \(24\%\) of the batch and a hundred times too many.

review.x: In a depot, \(15\%\) of the vehicles are vans and the rest are trucks, and there are 630 more trucks than vans. Enter the number of vehicles in the depot.
hints: Vans and trucks are the only two kinds, so the trucks are the remaining \(85\%\) of the same total.
With \(b\) the total, the gap is \(\frac{85}{100}b-\frac{15}{100}b\), which collects to \(\frac{70}{100}b\).
review.sol: Writing the total as \(b\), the vans number \(\frac{15}{100}b\) and the trucks \(\frac{85}{100}b\), so \(\frac{70}{100}b=630\) and \(b=\boxed{900}\). The check is \(135\) vans and \(765\) trucks, a gap of \(630\).

blocks.x: Lesson 6.3 turned every percent question into \(a=\frac{p}{100}b\), with one of the three quantities unknown. Here the amount itself changes. A rise or a fall of \(k\) percent is a change of \(\frac{k}{100}\) of the amount before it, so that earlier amount is the base. The first two problems take a rise of the same percent by two separate routes.

A quarry shipped 3400 tonnes of gravel in June, and July's shipment was 15 percent higher. Work it in two steps. Find 15 percent of 3400 first, then add that onto 3400, and enter July's shipment in tonnes.
accept: three thousand nine hundred and ten
hints: The 15 percent is measured against June's 3400 tonnes, so \(\frac{15}{100}(3400)\) is the size of the rise and not July's shipment.
Dividing 3400 by 100 leaves 34, so \(\frac{15}{100}(3400)\) is just \(15\times 34\). That result is what gets added onto 3400.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{15}{100}(3400)=510\), and \(3400+510=\boxed{3910}\). The percent is taken of June's shipment, so 3400 is the base and the 510 is the rise rather than the new total.

blocks.x: A second pit shipped 2600 tonnes in June, and its shipments rose 15 percent in July. July's shipment is \(2600+\frac{15}{100}(2600)\), and 2600 is a factor of both terms. Factor it out, do the one multiplication that remains, and enter July's shipment in tonnes.
hints: Both terms contain 2600, since \(2600=2600(1)\). Pulling a shared factor out front is the factoring of 2.3, the distributive property read right to left.
Factoring gives \(2600\left(1+\frac{15}{100}\right)\), and \(1+\frac{15}{100}\) is a single number.
blocks.sol: Factoring gives \(2600\left(1+\frac{15}{100}\right)=2600(1.15)=\boxed{2990}\). Going the long way, \(\frac{15}{100}(2600)=390\) and \(2600+390=2990\), so a 15 percent rise is one multiplication rather than a percent step followed by an addition.

blocks.x: The multiplier. Raising \(x\) by \(k\) percent gives \(x+\frac{k}{100}x\), and factoring the \(x\) out leaves \(x\left(1+\frac{k}{100}\right)\). Lowering \(x\) by \(k\) percent gives \(x-\frac{k}{100}x=x\left(1-\frac{k}{100}\right)\). The number inside the parentheses is the multiplier. Factoring works here because the percent is taken of \(x\) itself, so \(x\) is a common factor of both terms, and the whole change is then one multiplication instead of a percent step followed by an addition.
A pressroom used 5400 litres of ink last quarter and cut its use by 28 percent this quarter. Use one multiplication to find this quarter's ink use, and enter it in litres.
hints: A cut leaves part of the original, so the multiplier is below 1. Take 28 percent away from the whole 100 percent to see what percent of the ink is left.
The multiplier is \(1-\frac{28}{100}=0.72\), so the work is \(5400(0.72)\).
blocks.sol: \(5400\left(1-\frac{28}{100}\right)=5400(0.72)=\boxed{3888}\). Subtracting instead gives \(\frac{28}{100}(5400)=1512\) and \(5400-1512=3888\), the same number, because multiplying by \(0.72\) does that subtraction in one step.

blocks.x: A regional grid operator reports that this winter's peak demand was exactly 0.925 times last winter's peak. Enter the percent by which peak demand fell, a number only.
hints: Every fall multiplier has the form \(1-\frac{k}{100}\), so compare \(0.925\) with that form and read off what \(\frac{k}{100}\) has to be.
blocks.sol: A fall multiplier is \(1-\frac{k}{100}\), and \(1-0.925=0.075\), so \(k=100(0.075)=\boxed{7.5}\). Answering 92.5 gives the percent of last winter's peak that is left rather than the percent lost, and those two always total 100.

blocks.x: The multiplier is a single number. A rise of 9 percent is a multiplication by \(1.09\), and a fall of 3 percent is a multiplication by \(0.97\). Going the other way, \(1.04\) is \(1+\frac{4}{100}\), a rise of 4 percent, and \(0.78\) is \(1-\frac{22}{100}\), a fall of 22 percent. A multiplier above \(1\) is a rise, one below \(1\) is a fall, and \(1\) exactly is no change. The distance from \(1\) is the percent divided by \(100\), so a percent and its multiplier are two spellings of one fact and knowing one is knowing the other.

blocks.cap: The bar is the amount before the change. Putting a piece worth \(\frac{k}{100}\) of the bar on the end gives \(x+\frac{k}{100}x\), and cutting a piece of that same size off gives \(x-\frac{k}{100}x\). Factoring the \(x\) out of each leaves the two numbers on the card, and either change is one multiplication by one of them.

blocks.x: For two changes in a row, one multiplier is applied and then the other, so the amount ends at \(xm_1m_2\). Each change is a percent of the amount just before it, and after the first change that amount is no longer \(x\). The next two problems check whether the percents combine as simply as the multipliers do.
A workshop counted 6400 orders in June. The count rose 25 percent in July, then fell 25 percent in August, with the August fall taken off the July count. Enter the August order count.
hints: The July rise and the August fall are the same percent but not the same number of orders, since the August fall is 25 percent of the July count.
The July count is \(6400(1.25)\). Take 25 percent off that count, not off \(6400\).
blocks.sol: \(6400(1.25)=8000\), and \(8000(0.75)=\boxed{6000}\). The rise is \(1600\) orders and the fall is \(2000\) orders, since 25 percent of \(8000\) is more than 25 percent of \(6400\), so the August count is \(400\) below the June count.

blocks.x: A library's holdings grew 30 percent in one decade and 40 percent in the next, each rise measured against the holdings at the start of that decade. A clerk adds the percents and reports that the holdings are now 1.7 times the original. Enter the number the original holdings are actually multiplied by.
hints: The second rise is 40 percent of the holdings at the start of the second decade, not 40 percent of the original. Call the original holdings \(x\) and write what the holdings are after each decade.
A 30 percent rise multiplies by \(1.3\) and a 40 percent rise multiplies by \(1.4\), so the holdings come to \(x(1.3)(1.4)\), and a product can be regrouped.
blocks.sol: Writing the original holdings as \(x\), the first rise brings them to \(1.3x\) and the second brings them to \(1.4(1.3x)\), so the multiplier is \((1.3)(1.4)=\boxed{1.82}\). Adding the percents gives the clerk's 1.7 and leaves out the 40 percent taken on the first decade's growth, worth \(0.4(0.3x)=0.12x\), and \(1.7+0.12=1.82\).

blocks.x: Changes in a row multiply. Multiplying \(x\) by \(m_1\) and then by \(m_2\) gives \((xm_1)m_2\), and regrouping leaves \(x(m_1m_2)\), so the pair is one multiplication by \(m_1m_2\). The percents do not add, since the second one is taken of the amount after the first change and not of \(x\). A rise and then a fall of the same percent multiplies by a number below \(1\), since the fall is taken of the larger amount the rise produced, so the amount never returns to the start. A 25 percent rise then a 25 percent fall multiplies by \(1.25(0.75)=0.9375\).

Sometimes the amount after the change is given and the amount before it is wanted. The change is still one multiplication, so \(N=Om\), one equation with \(O\) unknown, and chapter 4 divides both sides by \(m\). Taking the same percent off \(N\) is a different calculation, since that percent was measured against \(O\) and \(N\) is not \(O\).

A season pass costs 336 dollars after a 12 percent rise. A student takes 12 percent off 336 and reports 295.68 dollars as the old price. Check that against the stated rise, then enter the correct old price in dollars.
hints: The 12 percent was a percent of the old price, not of 336, so name the old price \(p\) and write the rise as an equation in \(p\).
The stated fact is \(1.12p=336\), so divide both sides by 1.12.
blocks.sol: Naming the old price \(p\), the stated rise gives \(1.12p=336\), so \(p=\frac{336}{1.12}=\boxed{300}\). Raising the student's 295.68 by 12 percent gives 331.1616, not 336. The 12 percent belongs to the old price, so undoing the rise is a division by 1.12, and 0.88 is not \(\frac{1}{1.12}\).

blocks.x: The percent sign came out of handwriting rather than from any one inventor. Italian clerks wrote per cento, shortened that to a written per 100, and through the 1600s the shorthand collapsed until only the circles and slanted stroke of \(\%\) were left.

A factory's output fell 20 percent in the spring and then rose 5 percent in the summer, with each change measured against the output just before that change. Summer output was 8400 units a day. Enter the daily output, in units a day, before the 20 percent drop.
hints: Two changes in a row are one multiplication by the product of the two multipliers, so collapse the pair into a single multiplier before working backwards.
Write \(O\) for the daily output before the drop. Since \(0.8(1.05)=0.84\), the equation is \(0.84O=8400\).
blocks.sol: Writing \(O\) for the daily output before the drop, the two multipliers give \(0.8(1.05)=0.84\), so \(0.84O=8400\) and \(O=\frac{8400}{0.84}=\boxed{10000}\). Check forward, \(10000(0.8)=8000\) and \(8000(1.05)=8400\). A 20 percent drop then a 5 percent rise is not a 15 percent drop, since 0.84 is not 0.85.

blocks.x: Undoing a change is a division by the multiplier. From \(N=Om\), dividing both sides by \(m\) gives \(O=\frac{N}{m}\), which is chapter 4's move and not a new rule. Taking \(k\) percent off \(N\) instead multiplies by \(1-\frac{k}{100}\), and since \(\left(1+\frac{k}{100}\right)\left(1-\frac{k}{100}\right)\) is less than \(1\), that route gives a number smaller than the original every time. For two changes in a row, divide by the product \(m_1m_2\). The check is to run the stated changes forward on the recovered amount.

A percent change is the change measured against the amount before it, so from \(O\) to \(N\) the percent change is \(\frac{N-O}{O}\times 100\). The denominator is \(O\) every time. Swapping which of the two amounts comes first swaps the denominator, so the two directions between one fixed pair of amounts are different percents.

A workshop finished 450 units in March and 720 units in April. Find the percent increase from March to April, then find the percent decrease from April back down to March. Enter the percent increase minus the percent decrease.
hints: Both percents come from the same gap of 270 units, and they differ only in what that gap is divided by.
The increase is measured against March's 450, and the decrease is measured against April's 720.
blocks.sol: Up is \(\frac{270}{450}=0.6\), so 60 percent, and down is \(\frac{270}{720}=0.375\), so 37.5 percent, giving \(60-37.5=\boxed{22.5}\). The gap of 270 units is the same both ways and only the base changes, so the percent up and the percent back down are not equal.

blocks.x: A bakery cuts the price of a loaf by 10 percent and finds it then sells 30 percent more loaves. Revenue is price times number sold. No price and no number of loaves is stated anywhere, so write the old price as \(p\) and the old number sold as \(n\). Enter the percent by which revenue rises, a number only.
hints: Nothing pins down \(p\) or \(n\), so carry both letters and write the new revenue as the product of the two new quantities.
New revenue is \((0.9p)(1.3n)\). Compare that with the old revenue \(pn\), and see what is left once the letters cancel.
blocks.sol: New revenue is \((0.9p)(1.3n)=1.17pn\) against the old \(pn\), so \(\frac{1.17pn-pn}{pn}=0.17\) and the percent rise is \(\boxed{17}\). Both letters cancel, so the answer holds for every price and every number of loaves. Adding the percents to get 20 leaves out the 30 percent gain being counted on the reduced price.

blocks.x: The base of a percent change is the amount before it. The change from \(O\) to \(N\) is \(\frac{N-O}{O}\times 100\) percent, with \(O\) below the bar because the change is compared with where it started. Since \(\frac{N-O}{O}\) and \(\frac{N-O}{N}\) differ whenever \(O\) and \(N\) do, a rise between two amounts and the fall back are different percents. In a run of changes the base of each percent is the amount just before it, which is why the multipliers multiply. When no amount is stated, name the starting amount with a letter, and in a comparison built from it that letter cancels.

A mixture problem gives a percent for each ingredient and asks for a percent of the blend. Two percents cannot be averaged here, since each one is a percent of a different amount. The amounts of the substance itself do add, so count the litres of it on each side, total those, and divide by the total volume of the blend.

A bottler mixes 45 litres of a syrup that is 60 percent sugar with 75 litres of a syrup that is 20 percent sugar. Averaging the two percents gives 40, which is not the answer. Enter the percent sugar in the blend, a number only.
hints: The two percents are percents of different volumes, so they do not combine directly. Work out the litres of sugar in each syrup first.
The blend holds \(45(0.6)+75(0.2)\) litres of sugar in \(45+75\) litres of syrup.
blocks.sol: The sugar totals \(45(0.6)+75(0.2)=27+15=42\) litres in 120 litres of blend, and \(\frac{42}{120}=0.35\), so the percent sugar is \(\boxed{35}\). Averaging to get 40 would be right only for equal volumes, and here the weaker syrup is the larger batch, so the blend lands below the halfway mark.

blocks.x: A vat holds 280 litres of glaze that is 5 percent pigment by volume. Pure pigment is stirred in until the glaze is 30 percent pigment. One student pours in 70 litres, which is 25 percent of 280, reasoning that the percent has to go up by 25 points, and gets 24 percent instead. Enter the number of litres of pure pigment stirred in.
hints: Call the litres poured in \(a\). Every litre poured in is a litre of pigment and also a litre of glaze, so the pigment and the total both go up by \(a\).
The vat starts with \(0.05(280)=14\) litres of pigment, so the equation is \(\frac{14+a}{280+a}=0.3\).
blocks.sol: With \(a\) litres poured in, the pigment is \(0.05(280)+a=14+a\) and the total is \(280+a\), so \(\frac{14+a}{280+a}=0.3\). Cross-multiplying gives \(14+a=84+0.3a\), then \(0.7a=70\) and \(a=\boxed{100}\). Check, 114 litres of pigment in 380 litres of glaze is 30 percent. The 70-litre route gives \(\frac{84}{350}\), or 24 percent, because those 70 litres are part of the new total as well.

blocks.x: Every change here was one multiplication, two changes in a row were one multiplication by the product of the two multipliers, and going backwards was a division. Lesson 6.5, Direct and Inverse Proportion, looks at two quantities that change together. The question there is what stays fixed, a ratio in one case and a product in the other.

review.x: A walking trail is 1800 meters long and is lengthened by 10 percent. Enter the new length in meters.
accept: one thousand nine hundred and eighty
hints: The new length is the whole 1800 plus 10 percent of 1800, and 10 percent of a number is one tenth of it.
Adding a tenth of a number to itself is the same as multiplying by \(1+\frac{10}{100}=1.1\), so the work is \(1800(1.1)\).
review.sol: \(1800(1.1)=\boxed{1980}\). The increase alone is \(\frac{10}{100}(1800)=180\), and \(1800+180\) is the same length.

review.x: A farm harvested 5600 kilograms of barley last year, and this year's harvest fell 25 percent. Enter this year's harvest in kilograms.
hints: Taking 25 percent off the whole 100 percent leaves 75 percent of the harvest.
The multiplier is \(1-\frac{25}{100}=0.75\), so the work is \(5600(0.75)\).
review.sol: \(5600(0.75)=\boxed{4200}\). The fall itself is \(0.25(5600)=1400\), and \(5600-1400\) gives the same harvest.

review.x: A distributor multiplies every wholesale price by 1.06 to get the retail price. Enter the percent by which the retail price is above the wholesale price, a number only.
hints: A price that is \(k\) percent above another is \(1+\frac{k}{100}\) times it, so compare \(1.06\) with that form.
The part above 1 is \(1.06-1=0.06\), so write \(0.06\) as a number of hundredths.
review.sol: \(1.06=1+0.06=1+\frac{6}{100}\), so the percent rise is \(\boxed{6}\). The amount past 1 is the percent divided by 100, so \(0.06\) means 6 percent, while \(1.06\) itself is the retail price as 106 percent of the wholesale price.

review.x: A sale takes \(18\%\) off every price. Enter the single number that each original price is multiplied by to get the sale price.
hints: The number typed here has to turn a full price into a sale price, so it is less than \(1\). Ask what percent of the original price a shopper still pays.
Try a price of \(100\) and work out what that item costs on sale. Dividing that sale price by \(100\) gives the multiplier.
review.sol: After \(18\%\) comes off, \(100\%-18\%=82\%\) of the price remains, so the multiplier is \(1-0.18=\boxed{0.82}\). The value \(0.18\) is the size of the discount, not the share of the price still paid.

review.x: A club grew from 250 members to 315 members. Enter the percent increase, a number only.
hints: A percent increase is the change divided by the amount before the change, so the base here is 250 and not 315.
The change is \(315-250=65\), so write \(\frac{65}{250}\) as a decimal and then as a percent.
review.sol: The change is \(315-250=65\), and \(\frac{65}{250}=0.26\), so the percent increase is \(\boxed{26}\). Dividing by the new 315 instead gives about 20.6 percent, which compares the change to the final size rather than the starting size.

review.x: A commute that took 105 minutes now takes 84 minutes. Enter the percent decrease, a number only.
hints: Percent change is measured against the amount you started with, which is 105 minutes.
Subtract to find the drop in minutes, then divide that drop by 105 and write the decimal as a percent.
review.sol: The drop is \(105-84=21\) minutes, and \(\frac{21}{105}=0.2\), so the percent decrease is \(\boxed{20}\). Check, \(105(0.8)=84\).

review.x: After an 8 percent rise, the rent on an apartment is 1350 dollars a month. Enter the monthly rent in dollars before the rise.
accept: one thousand two hundred and fifty
hints: The 8 percent was a percent of the old rent, so name the old rent \(r\) and write the new rent in terms of \(r\).
The equation is \(1.08r=1350\), so divide both sides by \(1.08\).
review.sol: \(1.08r=1350\) gives \(r=\frac{1350}{1.08}=\boxed{1250}\). Check, \(1250(1.08)=1350\). Taking 8 percent off \(1350\) gives \(1242\), which is not the old rent, since the 8 percent is a percent of the smaller old rent rather than of \(1350\).

review.x: A bus fare is cut by 35 percent, and the new fare is 26 dollars. Enter the fare in dollars before the cut.
hints: A 35 percent cut takes away 35 percent of the old fare and leaves 65 percent of it.
Call the old fare \(f\). The 26 dollars is \(0.65f\), so the equation reads \(0.65f=26\).
review.sol: Let \(f\) be the old fare. A 35 percent cut leaves \(1-0.35=0.65\) of it, so \(0.65f=26\) and \(f=\frac{26}{0.65}=\boxed{40}\). Adding 35 percent of \(26\) back on gives \(35.10\), not \(40\), because that 35 percent would be a share of the smaller new fare rather than of the old one.

review.x: An amount \(x\) rises by 50 percent. The new amount then falls by 30 percent of itself. The ending amount equals \(mx\) for a single number \(m\). Enter \(m\) as a decimal.
hints: Write each change as a multiplier applied to whatever amount is present at that moment. A rise of 50 percent multiplies by \(1.5\).
Taking away 30 percent leaves 70 percent, so the ending amount is \(x(1.5)(0.7)\) and \(m\) is that product.
review.sol: The two multipliers give \(m=1.5\times 0.7=\boxed{1.05}\). That is a net rise of 5 percent, not the 20 percent that subtracting the percents suggests, since the 30 percent is taken from the raised amount rather than from \(x\).

review.x: A crowd of 5200 grows 45 percent by noon and then shrinks 40 percent by evening. Enter the evening crowd size.
accept: four thousand five hundred twenty four
hints: The 40 percent is taken off the noon crowd, so work the two changes in order.
Noon is \(5200(1.45)\), and evening is that count multiplied by \(0.6\).

review.x: A stock of parts falls 10 percent one month and 10 percent again the next. Enter the overall percent change, a number only, with a minus sign if it is a fall.
hints: The second 10 percent is taken off the reduced stock, not off the original.
A 10 percent fall multiplies the amount by \(0.9\), so two of them multiply by \(0.9(0.9)=0.81\). The overall change is how far \(0.81\) sits from \(1\), written as a percent.
review.sol: Two 10 percent falls multiply the stock by \(0.9(0.9)=0.81\), and \(0.81\) is \(0.19\) less than \(1\), a fall of \(19\) percent, so the overall percent change is \(\boxed{-19}\). The second 10 percent comes off the reduced stock, so two 10 percent falls land short of a 20 percent fall.

review.x: Store B sells a tool for 20 percent less than store A charges for the same tool. Enter the percent by which store A's price is above store B's price, a number only.
hints: No price is given for either store, so name store A's price \(a\) and write store B's price in terms of \(a\).
Store B's price is \(0.8a\). A percent above store B's price is measured against store B's price, not against store A's.
review.sol: Call store A's price \(a\), so store B's price is \(0.8a\) and the gap is \(a - 0.8a = 0.2a\). Measured against store B's price, that gap is \(\frac{0.2a}{0.8a} = 0.25\), so the answer is \(\boxed{25}\). The \(a\) drops out of the ratio, so the same percent holds for any price, and the two directions differ only because one comparison uses \(a\) as its base and the other uses \(0.8a\).

review.x: An amount is raised by 150 percent. Enter the percent of the new amount that must then be taken off to return to the original amount, a number only.
hints: A 150 percent rise is the same as multiplying by one number. Find that number before thinking about the cut.
Multiplying by \(2.5\) is undone by multiplying by \(\frac{1}{2.5}\), so write that as a decimal and compare it with \(1\).
review.sol: Raising by 150 percent means multiplying by \(1+\frac{150}{100}=2.5\), and undoing that means multiplying by \(\frac{1}{2.5}=0.4\), so the percent taken off is \(\boxed{60}\). Taking off 150 percent would leave a negative amount, so the percent taken off is never equal to the percent added.

review.x: In a survey, 60 percent of the people asked own a bicycle, and 45 percent of those bicycle owners also own a helmet. The number of people asked is not given. Enter the percent of all the people asked who own both a bicycle and a helmet, a number only.
hints: The 45 percent is a percent of the bicycle owners, not of everyone asked, so the two bases are different.
With \(n\) people asked, the owners number \(0.6n\), and the helmet owners among them number \(0.45(0.6n)\).
review.sol: With \(n\) people asked, the number who own both is \(0.45(0.6n)=0.27n\), so the percent is \(\boxed{27}\). The \(n\) cancels, so the answer does not depend on how many people were asked. Adding to get 105 or averaging to get 52.5 both treat the two percents as though they had the same base.

review.x: A blender combines 24 liters of a mix that is 70 percent apple juice with 56 liters of a mix that is 30 percent apple juice. Enter the percent apple juice in the combined mix, a number only.
hints: Count the liters of apple juice in each batch separately rather than combining the two percents.
The apple juice comes to \(24(0.7)+56(0.3)\) liters, and the combined mix comes to \(80\) liters.
review.sol: The apple juice totals \(24(0.7)+56(0.3)=16.8+16.8=33.6\) liters in \(80\) liters of mix, and \(\frac{33.6}{80}=0.42\), so the percent apple juice is \(\boxed{42}\). Averaging 70 and 30 gives 50, which would be right only if the two batches were the same size.

review.x: A tank contains 150 liters of a solution that is 12 percent acid by volume. Pure acid is added until the solution is 20 percent acid. Enter the number of liters of pure acid added.
hints: Every liter added is a liter of acid and also a liter of solution, so name the amount added \(a\) and write the new acid amount and the new total in terms of it.
The tank starts with \(0.12(150)=18\) liters of acid, so set the new acid amount over the new total equal to \(0.2\).
review.sol: The tank starts with \(0.12(150)=18\) liters of acid, and adding \(a\) liters of pure acid gives \(\frac{18+a}{150+a}=0.2\), so \(18+a=30+0.2a\), then \(0.8a=12\) and \(a=\boxed{15}\). Check, 33 liters of acid in 165 liters is 20 percent.

review.x: A machine's price rose 20 percent in the spring and fell 15 percent in the autumn, and it now costs 2040 dollars. Enter its price in dollars before the spring rise.
hints: Rising 20 percent multiplies the price by \(1.2\), and falling 15 percent multiplies by \(0.85\). Doing one and then the other is a single multiplication.
Let \(p\) be the price before the rise. Since \(1.2(0.85)=1.02\), the equation is \(1.02p=2040\).
review.sol: Let \(p\) be the price before the rise. The two changes collapse to one multiplier, \(1.2(0.85)=1.02\), so \(1.02p=2040\) and \(p=\frac{2040}{1.02}=\boxed{2000}\). Check forward, \(2000(1.2)=2400\) and \(2400(0.85)=2040\). A 20 percent rise and a 15 percent fall leave the price 2 percent up, not 5 percent up.
